newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Vienna landmine ban forum hailed a success.
newsitem.headline: Vienna landmine ban forum hailed a success.

text.p: Governments and pressure groups on Friday hailed as a success a forum, hosted by Austria, to start the ball rolling for a total ban on land mines worldwide.
"The world is inexorably on the path to a total ban on anti-personnel mines," Jody Williams, International Campaign to Ban Landmines (ICBL) coordinator, said in a statement.
"This conference has demonstrated that a large number of governments will be prepared to sign a ban treaty before the end of the year," she said.
The three-day conference, which ended on Friday and was attended by over 100 government experts, was part of the so-called "Ottawa process" begun last October at a 50-nation forum hosted by Canada.
The Canadian government has the ambitious aim of achieving a legally-binding agreement by December 1997 to ban the production, stockpiling, export, and use of land mines.
Over 100 million land mines lie buried in 64 countries around the world. According to U.N. statistics land mines kill or maim a person every 20 minutes, or 25,000 people a year.

Thomas Hajnoczi, head of disarmament at the Austrian foreign ministry and chairman of the forum, told a news briefing organised by the ICBL, that the draft from the forum could be the basis for future negotiations.

"It was the first time we have had a broad formal exchange of views on the content of such a convention (to ban land mines)," he said. "One theme that came up again and again was the urgency and significance of going for a total ban."
But Cuba, Ecuador, South Korea and Sri Lanka said they would continue to use land mines for security, the ICBL said.
Jill Sinclair, head of disarmament at Canada's foreign ministry, said: "The practical work has begun and this is a most important step."

The U.N.-sponsored Conference on Disarmament in Geneva, which has 61 members including Russia and China -- two top mine producers and exporters -- is expected to start up its own separate initiative on land mines within the next two months.
Many governments -- including the United States, Britain, France and Italy -- said they preferred the step-by-step approach of the Geneva body, which will meet three times this year, the ICBL said.
China and Russia have not participated in the "Ottawa talks", although India, Pakistan, Russia and Ukraine were present at the Vienna forum as observers.

"It is our view that nations advocating the Conference for Disarmament and a step-by-step approach are not really prepared to match their rhetoric of a world free of antipersonnel mines with the actions necessary to ban this indiscriminate killer as soon as possible," the ICBL's Williams said.
There are over 360 different types of anti-personnel mines, which explode underfoot, as opposed to anti-armour mines, designed to go off under the weight of heavy vehicles.
A follow-up conference is planned in Brussels in June before a December meeting in Ottawa.
